newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia 1997 money policy seen tight.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia 1997 money policy seen tight.

text.p: The National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) will pursue a tight monetary policy in 1997 and keep a firm grip on its key M1 money supply during the first quarter this year, NBY Vice-Governor Ratko Banovic said Thursday.
"Monetary policy must remain tight. But a degree of restrictiveness will vary depending on overall economic activity, Yugoslavia's ties with the world and its return to world markets,".

"It is clear that money policy will be very restrictive during the first quarter. We must keep M1 at the December 31, 1996, level. This is the only way to keep the dinar stable and halt price increases," Banovic told Reuters in an interview.

According to the central bank figures, M1 money supply stood at 5.5 billion dinars ($1.008 billion) at the end of December. This is slightly down on 5.72 billion dinars estimated by independent analysts.
The central bank planned to stick to the currency board mechanism of creating base money. "Any increase in the base money must have hard currency backing," Banovic said.
Monetary policy calculations were based on the dinar exchange rate fixed at 3.3 to the German mark. In the meantime, the dinar has slipped to 3.8 on the black market.
At the same time, the local interbank forex market will remain open to all clients in need of hard currency.
NBY plans no changes in its discount rate policy and signalled it would be more generous to those commercial banks following suit and adjusting the level of their lending rates to the NBY's key rate.
The discount rate will remain positive in real terms and will depend on retail price increases and interest rates on the local financial market.
"But commercial banks will have to follow suit if they want NBY to help at times of liquidity crisis," Banovic said.

The central bank first cut its key discount rate last June to 4.5 percent per month (68.15 percent a year), from 6.31 percent in May, in an attempt to push commercial lending rates lower. The discount rate remained unchanged in January for the eighth consecutive month.
Weighted commercial lending rates on short-term loans stood at an annual 216.53 percent in November. At the same time, average deposit rates were 34.3 percent a year.
"Banks seem to care only about lending rates and neglect interest rates on deposits. They narrow scope of their activity and discourage clients from depositing money," Banovic said.
"There will be no administrative control of interest rates, but those who follow, will have an advantage."
The central bank has also decided to use reserve requirement in regulating money supply in 1997.

"Last year, the reserve requirement served only to maintain liquidity of banks. But in 1997 it will fully serve to regulate money supply. There will be sanctions for those who do not set aside required amounts," Banovic said.
NBY abandoned the reserve requirement early in 1995 after banks had insisted they needed no regulation to establish their own reserves.

But during the first half of 1996, the first signs of liquidity problems appeared and late in August NBY decided to relaunch the reserve requirement and set it at 10 percent. It was raised to 15 percent in November.

"It turned out we were right. If we hadn't mopped up surplus liquidity in September and October and transferred it to the central bank, commercial banks would have faced serious problems at the end of December."
Banovic said the instrument was now completed.
The reserve requirement is set to remain unchanged at 15 percent in February. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
